--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.astar_path()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Find a shortest path with the A\* search algorithm. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.astar_path()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Find a shortest path with the A\* search algorithm. title: >- [Graph.astar_path()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Find a shortest path with the A\* search algorithm. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find a shortest path with the A* search algorithm. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L69193-L69320){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.astar_path( source, target, heuristic=None, weighted=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![A* path](../assets/graphs/astar-path.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A six-by-six grid searched from its top-left corner (0,0) to the bottom-right corner (5,5), outlined. Each node is labeled with the Manhattan-distance heuristic h, its estimated remaining distance to the target, from 10 down to 0. The returned shortest path, 10 hops along the top row and down the right column, is in the accent color; along it the steps taken plus h always sum to 10." width="100%"} A* is Dijkstra's algorithm steered by a *heuristic*: an estimate of the remaining distance from a node to the target. Nodes that look closer to the target are explored first, so with a good estimate A* finds the same shortest path after visiting far fewer nodes. It is the standard algorithm for route planning on road networks and maps, game and robot path finding, and puzzle solving, where a natural estimate exists (straight- line distance, Manhattan distance on a grid, number of misplaced tiles). The heuristic must never overestimate the true remaining distance (it must be *admissible*); otherwise the path may not be shortest. Without a heuristic, A* is exactly Dijkstra's algorithm. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The endpoints, as IDs or labels. [target]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The endpoints, as IDs or labels. [heuristic]{.doc-parameter-name}[=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op}[None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional function `heuristic(node_id, target_id) -> float` estimating the distance from a node to the target. If `None` (default), every estimate is `0`. [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to use edge weights. If `None` (default), follows the graph's `weighted` flag. Weights must be non-negative. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int] or None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node IDs of a shortest path from `source` to `target`, or `None` if the target cannot be reached. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a node does not exist or a weight is negative. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} A* (Hart, Nilsson and Raphael, 1968) pops nodes in order of $g(v) + h(v)$, the distance so far plus the estimate. With an admissible and consistent $h$ the first time the target is popped its distance is optimal, and the number of nodes expanded never exceeds Dijkstra's. The heuristic is called once per discovered node (results are cached). The path length agrees with NetworkX's `astar_path_length`. ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~astar_path_length`) : The length of the path alone. [](`~alt_heuristic`) : An admissible heuristic built from landmarks. [](`~ada_star_search`) : A* with an inflated heuristic for a quicker answer. [](`~shortest_path`) : Dijkstra's algorithm, with no heuristic. ## Examples {.doc-examples} On a 6 x 6 grid with Manhattan distance as the heuristic, A* walks straight toward the corner: ::: {#28cf2f35 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec grid = ec.Graph().add_grid_2d(6, 6) ids = sorted(grid.get_node_ids(limit=None)) position = {n: divmod(i, 6) for i, n in enumerate(ids)} def manhattan(node, target): (r1, c1), (r2, c2) = position[node], position[target] return abs(r1 - r2) + abs(c1 - c2) path = grid.astar_path(ids[0], ids[-1], heuristic=manhattan) len(path) - 1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 10 ``` ::: ::: ### Heading for the destination on the metro `metro()` is a made-up city's metro network, with each stretch of track weighted by its travel time in minutes. No stretch takes fewer minutes than its straight-line length on the map of station positions, so the straight-line distance to the destination never overestimates the time left, and A* with it finds a fastest route: ::: {#e6e43c35 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import math metro = ec.metro() nodes = metro.get_node_df() pos = {n: tuple(p) for n, p in zip(nodes["id"], nodes["pos"])} def straight_line(node, target): return math.dist(pos[node], pos[target]) route = metro.astar_path("Westgate", "Airport", heuristic=straight_line) [metro.get_label_from_id(n) for n in route] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['Westgate', 'Mill Lane', 'Old Town', 'Central', 'Market', 'Eastfield', 'Business Park', 'Airport'] ``` ::: ::: ### Fastest or fewest stops To Lakeside, the fastest route runs through the center in 18 minutes: ::: {#e9d9bc84 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} fastest = metro.astar_path( "Westgate", "Lakeside", heuristic=straight_line ) metro.plot(layout="pos", highlight=fastest, label_by="label") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: With `weighted=False`, A* counts stops instead, and the route takes the Green line around the north: four stops rather than six, but 22 minutes. The heuristic is left out here, since a distance in minutes can overestimate a count of stops: ::: {#cd597b00 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} fewest = metro.astar_path("Westgate", "Lakeside", weighted=False) metro.plot(layout="pos", highlight=fewest, label_by="label") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: [Paths and distances](../user-guide/paths.qmd#a-search) steers A* across a road network with the straight-line distance between cities.
